---
title: "Abstract"
author: 
    - "Kayla Tillmon"
---
This project examines the similarities and differences in how Black individuals experience the criminal legal system across the DMV area. Although these three places are geographically close, they have different populations, legal structures, and criminal justice systems. Using incarceration data from 2013 to 2021, population data from NHGIS, D.C. adult arrest data, and federal sentencing data. I examine the racial representation across multiple parts of the legal system. My results show that the interpretation of racial disparity changes on how it is measured. D.C. had the highest Black share of its incarcerated population, but Virginia has the highest Black incarceration overrepresentation when each state's overall Black population was taken into account. D.C. arrest data also showed high amounts of Black representation across the top 20 most commen arrest categories, while using a common framework of federal sentencing showed that Virginia had the longest median imprisonment length, in months, for Black convicted and sentenced firearm offenses. Overall, the findings show that the main similarity across these three jurisdictions is that Black individuals are highly represented across the legal system, while the differences lie in how and where that high representation shows up. This suggests that geography continues to affect the Black experience within the criminal legal system. In a future iteration of this project, I would plan to look at arrest data from across all three states, not just D.C., and expand the sentencing analysis to additional offense categories, specifically drug offenses.
